newsitem.title: UK: Full text of Feb UK purchasing managers' survey.
newsitem.headline: Full text of Feb UK purchasing managers' survey.

text.p: Following is the full text of the February Report on Business (Purchasing Managers' Survey) of the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS):
OUTPUT AND ORDERS SHOW STRONG GAINS DESPITE WEAKER GROWTH OF EXPORT DEMAND. PRICES INDEX FALLS FOR SIXTEENTH CONSECUTIVE MONTH.
UK purchasing managers reported a further expansion of manufacturing activity in February.

The seasonally adjusted Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI - a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of manufacturing activity) remained well above the 50.0 "no change" level in February, signalling expansion for the ninth consecutive month. The index dipped slightly, however, pointing to a very slight easing in the rate of growth.

The continued expansion of the manufacturing economy largely reflected a strong rise in output during the month. Output recorded the fastest growth since November 1994 as firms cleared backlogs of orders and rebuilt stocks of finished goods which had again been depleted through sales exceeding output.
The rate of growth of new orders also remained strong but slowed slightly, leading to the modest weakening of the PMI.

This slower rate of increase of orders was principally linked to export performance. Orders from UK customers were reported to have remained buoyant but export orders grew only modestly. The continued strength of the pound, by making UK goods more expensive in overseas markets, was increasingly being blamed for lost orders.

On the other side of the coin, however, the strength of the pound continued to bring advantages to producers in the form of reduced prices for imported inputs. Measured overall, input prices fell for the sixteenth consecutive month in February and registered the sharpest monthly fall since last July. Nearly a third of all purchasing managers reported lower average prices.

Suppliers' delivery times also pointed to relatively subdued inflationary pressures. In spite of growing demand for inputs (the quantity of goods purchased rose in February), delivery times lengthened only modestly. Less than 8% of suppliers experienced delays in meeting demand for their finished goods. Finally, the PMI was also weakened slightly by a moderate decline in the rate of growth of employment. Recruitment of new staff has been slow in manufacturing since 1994 and continues to be subdued by rationalisation programmes intended to boost efficiency. * The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing economy and acts as a leading indicator for the whole economy. The indicator is derived from individual diffusion indices which measure changes in output, new orders, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of goods purchased. A reading of the PMI below 50% indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining; above 50%, that it is generally expanding. The seasonally adjusted index may be subject to revision as improved estimation of seasonal adjustments occur with each month's new data.
OUTPUT

The seasonally adjusted Output index rose in February, recording the fastest rate of growth since November 1994. Output growth has been on a firmly upward trend over the past nine months as firms have reacted to rising demand. Output of consumer, investment and intermediate goods all rose in February, with intermediate goods (components) showing the greatest increase for the second month running.
NEW ORDERS

New orders rose strongly in February, the ninth consecutive monthly increase. The rate of growth dipped very slightly after seasonal adjustment. Although demand from UK markets remained buoyant, growth of export demand weakened. The strength of sterling was reported to have reduced the competitiveness of UK goods abroad, especially consumer goods.
QUANTITY OF PURCHASES

The quantity of goods purchased increased in February as firms expanded output to meet growth of orders. However, purchasing managers deliberately bought fewer inputs than were required for current growth of output in order to run down stock holdings and thereby improve cash flow.
PRICES

The seasonally adjusted Prices Index recorded the largest monthly drop in the prices paid for inputs since last July. Just over 30% of companies reported lower prices in February. The key factor behind the latest fall was the reduced cost of imported goods and raw materials arising from the continued strength of sterling. Weak world-wide demand for commodities also helped to maintain a buyers' market.
SUPPLIERS' DELIVERY TIMES

The Suppliers' Delivery Times Index remained below 50.0 in February, indicating lengthening delivery times for the sixth month in a row. Delays were incurred in supplying goods due to low stock holdings and an inability of some suppliers to raise output capacity to meet demand in the short-term. However, the relatively low incidence of delays suggests few inflationary pressures were being generated by capacity constraints.
STOCKS OF PURCHASES

Stocks of purchases fell in February, largely due to intentional destocking policies: Increased output led to greater usage of raw material stock holdings during the month which were not fully replaced due to the continued desire to run down stock levels for cost considerations. Such destocking has been associated partly with the reduced need to hold safety stocks in the light of good availability of cheap supplies.
STOCKS OF FINISHED GOODS

Stocks of finished goods fell in February and, after seasonal adjustment, the decline was of a similar magnitude to that seen in January. In spite of an increase in the number of companies reported to have been rebuilding stock levels to prepare for strong growth in sales over recent months, high sales levels were again the predominant cause of the latest decline in finished goods stock.
EMPLOYMENT

Seasonally adjusted employment rose for the seventh successive month in February, although the rate of growth slipped to produce only a modest increase during the month. Despite many firms recruiting to expand production capacity, the index continues to be subdued by on-going redundancy programmes intended to improve efficiencies and competitiveness.
INDICES BY MARKET SECTOR
CONSUMER GOODS (PANEL WEIGHT 30.5 PERCENT)

Output of consumer goods rose sharply again in February at a rate of growth similar to that recorded in the previous month. Additional output was required to reduce backlogs of orders and meet further growth of demand, but the rate of growth of new orders fell to the lowest level recorded since December 1995. This was largely due to a decline in export orders resulting from the strength of sterling. Input prices fell sharply again (the seventeenth month running) and suppliers' delivery times lengthened only modestly, suggesting a lack of inflationary pressures. The quantity of goods purchased registered only moderate growth, reflecting an increase in the number of companies planning to reduce stock levels in coming months.
INVESTMENT/CAPITAL GOODS (PANEL WEIGHT 23.3 PERCENT)

Producers of investment goods were the only companies to see a strengthening of export demand in February, which provided a further boost to growth of total order levels. Output rose sharply to meet the new business, registering the largest monthly rise since January 1995. More inputs were purchased to support the faster rate of production and the prices paid for prices fell sharply. The strength of the pound was reported to have again reduced the cost of imported goods. Suppliers' delivery times lengthened moderately for the third consecutive month, reflecting some capacity problems arising from the growth of demand. Stronger than anticipated demand also led to an overall decline in stocks of finished goods.
INTERMEDIATE GOODS (PANEL WEIGHT 46.2 PERCENT)

Output of intermediate goods recorded the fastest growth of all three Report on Business market sectors in February. The Output Index rose to its highest level since November 1994. Growth of new orders remained buoyant despite a slight drop in export orders. The strength of the pound was linked to the deterioration in overseas demand, but also had the advantage of causing a marked drop in prices of imported goods. The Prices Index registered the sharpest drop since last July as a result. Stocks of finished goods fell again, largely due to an inability of producers to meet rising demand with sufficient output. Some suppliers to these producers were reported to have been having similar problems, leading to a further lengthening of delivery times.
